Hi Samir / Amit,

Thanks again for the call earlier — good discussion and appreciate you walking us through the high-level SLOs. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we can kick off the private/VPC perf qualification: 

Recap (from our notes):
- P50 latency target: <= 50ms for short prompt flows (<= 128 tokens)
- P95 latency target: <= 200ms for typical interactive workloads
- Peak concurrency: 300 concurrent streaming sessions (audio->LLM transcription + streaming responses)
- Sustained throughput target: ~1,000 requests/minute with bursts to 2,500 RPM
- Streaming: chunked output expected every ~150-300ms per client; websocket or SSE preferred
- Deployment: Private VPC in us-east-1; Acme prefers VPC peering over public egress where possible

Open/clarifying items for us to validate:
1) Network path: do you plan to peer Acme VPC directly to Redwood's VPC, or will traffic traverse a NAT/GW and public egress?
2) Egress/IP constraints: any strict IP allowlists or static egress IPs required from Acme?
3) Internal latency budget: what is your target RTT from app servers to edge/bastion for calling APIs (ms)?
4) MTU or VPN limits (if using IPSec): any non-standard MTU or MSS in your tunnels?

Next steps we propose:
- Acme shares VPC peering / network config spreadsheet (we can use your existing sheet) — Samir/Amit
- Redwood provides a lightweight network test plan (traceroute/tcp_ping/iperf) and perf harness instructions — Marissa/Jordan (attached)
- Run a short network check (endpoints + 3x traceroutes) and share results — Target by 10/07
- Schedule 1-hour lab session for perf run (Redwood-run with Acme test tokens) — propose 10/08 or 10/09

Attachments: redwood_network_test_plan.pdf (test steps + sample output)

If that all looks right, can you share the VPC config and a preferred time for the lab session?

Hi Samir — Marissa,

Quick technical notes from the Redwood runtime side to help with the lab: 

- Preferred path: VPC peering (private) — avoids public NAT egress variability and keeps RTTs low.
- Expected intra-region baseline: if peered in us-east-1 we typically observe 1-4ms additional RTT between customer app hosts and our inference frontends (depending on AZ placement). That aligns with a target inference hop median of ~10-20ms on optimized paths; your 30ms median budget is workable.
- Concurrency and streaming: for streaming scenarios we advise websocket + per-chunk acking disabled (client should accept best-effort chunking). We aim to push the next chunk within 150-300ms; network jitter >100ms will impact user-perceived latency.
- TCP tuning: please ensure typical AWS ENA/GRO settings and allow MSS ~1400 when peering; if your apps sit behind a NAT GW that does MSS clamping it can add 10-30ms at high packet rates.
- MTU: if any tunnels are in the path (e.g., transit gateways + VPNs) and MTU < 1500, packet fragmentation can cause increased per-packet latency — note you mentioned 1400 for the legacy tunnel. Good to document which subnets will traverse which path.

For the perf lab, it will help if you can provide:
1) traceroute from a representative app host to the planned peering route (two AZs)
2) tcp_ping or hping3 at different packet sizes to see MSS/mss_clamp effects
3) a short pcap (15s) during a small load test if allowed (captures can be sanitized)

We'll run a baseline Redwood perf harness (100 concurrent sessions ramp to 300) and stream responses to measure chunk latency distribution, p50/p95 token latency, and retransmits.

-Jordan
Senior SRE, Redwood Inference
